title: Abhirama Thakura
html:
Ramadasa, Whose Life Was Nityananda

When the companions of Nityananda Prabhu are listed, the first named is usually Abhirama Thakura. Krishnadasa Kaviraja calls him “Ramadasa Abhirama” and “Sri Ramadasa,” Vrindavana Dasa “Ramadasa” and “Ramadasa Mahashaya,” Kavi Karnapura “the great Abhirama.” In the “Bhakti-ratnakara” he is “Abhirama Gopala,” “Sri Thakura Abhirama” and “Abhirama Gosvami”; Lochana Dasa too calls him “Abhirama Gosvami,” and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati in his “Anubhashya” calls him “Sri Ramadasa (Abhirama)” and “Thakura Abhirama.” The biographies also know him as Sri Abhirama Gopala Thakura and as Abhirama Dasa.1

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta says of him that he was one “whose very life was Nityananda” (nityanandaika-prana); the biographies call him Nityananda's dearest devotee. Vrindavana Dasa, listing Nityananda's companions, puts Ramadasa Mahashaya at their head (CB, Antya 5.722),2 and the “Bhakti-ratnakara” tells how from time to time Nityananda came with His companions to the house of His dear Abhirama (4.120).

Of the outward circumstances of his life little is known. According to the “Bhakti-ratnakara,” he “descended in a brahmana's house to deliver living beings” (4.105), and his disciple Vedagarbha Acharya calls him “the crest-jewel of brahmanas” (4.112). The sources name neither his birthplace nor his parents, nor the year and day of his appearance; nor is the day of his appearance found in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math.

Shridama

Who he is in Krishna's eternal pastimes, Kavi Karnapura tells us:

“He who was formerly called Shridama is now the great Abhirama; it was he who carried a log that only thirty-two men could lift.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 126)

This verse is quoted both by Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya” and by the biographies. Shridama is a cowherd friend of Krishna, one of those with whom He tends the calves in Vraja. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” says the same: an old brahmana of Khanakula tells Srinivasa that Thakura Abhirama “is, in Krishna's pastimes, the famous Shridama,” and that even now “he has revealed that former nature,” appearing to a certain servant in the form of Shridama (4.109–110). The same book quotes a verse by his disciple Vedagarbha Acharya:

“I worship the venerable Abhirama, formerly called Shridama, the embodiment of love, the crest-jewel of brahmanas, the husband of Sri Malini.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 4.112)

The “Vaishnava-vandana” also calls him Shridama (1.95, 5.72). Shridama did not “turn into” Abhirama: the eternal friend of Krishna descended into Gaura's pastimes together with the Lord, and his nature remained what it always was.

With the verse about him Karnapura opens his list of the friends of Vraja who descended with Nityananda (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 126–133). These companions of Nityananda are the twelve gopalas, and in the lists of one of the biographies Abhirama stands first; the “Anubhashya” on CC, Adi 11.13 calls him just so: “Thakura Abhirama (gopala 1).”

Krishnadasa Kaviraja counts him both as a branch of Sri Chaitanya's tree (Adi 10.116) and as one of the chief branches of Nityananda:

“Ramadasa, a chief branch, was a treasury of loving friendship. He lifted a log that it took sixteen men to carry and made a flute of it.” (CC, Adi 11.16)

A Treasury of Loving Friendship

What defines Abhirama is his love for Krishna as a friend (sakhya-prema). It explains his most famous wonder as well. Krishnadasa Kaviraja speaks of it twice; in the list of Sri Chaitanya's branches:

“Ramadasa Abhirama was a treasury of loving friendship. He lifted a log that it took sixteen men to carry and made a flute of it.” (CC, Adi 10.116)

and again in the list of Nityananda's branches, in the verse quoted above (Adi 11.16).

How it happened the “Bhakti-ratnakara” relates (4.121–124). Once Abhirama, intoxicated with love, was dancing. Absorbed in sakhya-rasa, he wished to play the flute and looked for it everywhere, but could not find it. Then

“a log that even a hundred men could not move he took in his hand as a flute.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 4.123)

All who saw it were amazed; and “such unearthly pastimes are always happening with him,” the narrator adds. The “Vaishnava-vandana” says that he lifted the sixteen-man log with two fingers.3

The source of this strength is not bodily might. The cowherd boy Shridama is looking for something to play for his Friend, and in the fullness of his love the log becomes a flute.

With Nityananda to Gauda

While Mahaprabhu was living in Puri, He told Nityananda to go to Gauda and give love for Krishna to everyone without distinction:

“To Nityananda He gave this order: ‘Go to Gauda and reveal loving devotion freely, without restraint. I am sending Ramadasa, Gadadhara and a few others along to help You.’” (CC, Madhya 15.42–43)

In the list of branches Krishnadasa Kaviraja names three:

“At the Lord's command Nityananda went to Gauda, and by the Lord's command three devotees went with Him: Sri Ramadasa, Madhava and Vasudeva Ghosha. Govinda stayed with the Lord, and was overjoyed to do so.” (CC, Adi 10.117–118)

According to the “Anubhashya” (on Adi 10.53), this was in the Shaka year 1434, about 1512–1513.

That is why Abhirama belongs to two circles at once, Sri Chaitanya's and Nityananda's:

“Sri Ramadasa and Gadadhara Dasa, devotees of Chaitanya Gosani, stayed at Nityananda's side. When Mahaprabhu told Nityananda to go to Gauda, He sent these two with Him. Therefore they are counted in both groups, and so it is with Madhava and Vasudeva Ghosha.” (CC, Adi 11.13–15)

Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura explains in the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya”: “Ramadasa is Abhirama dasa.”4

Vrindavana Dasa names the other companions on that journey:

“With Nityananda went Ramadasa, Gadadhara Dasa, Raghunatha Vaidya, full of the sweetness of loving devotion, Krishnadasa Pandita, Parameshvari Dasa and the jubilant Purandara Pandita.” (CB, Antya 5.231–233)

The “Bhakti-ratnakara” remembers it so too: “to Gauda goes Nityananda, and with Him Abhirama, Dasa Gadadhara and others” (12.3611).

Already on the road love seized them all, and in each his eternal mood came forth. First of all in Ramadasa:

“Ramadasa, the foremost of devotees, was the first to show the mood of a cowherd boy. On the way he stood bent in three places, and for nine hours he lost all awareness of the outer world.” (CB, Antya 5.236–237)

Later, listing Nityananda's companions, Vrindavana Dasa speaks of him again in particular:

“His chief companion was Ramadasa Mahashaya, who always spoke in the mood of the Lord. Not everyone could grasp the meaning of his words. Nityananda always dwelt in his heart. Of all the devotees Ramadasa was the most deeply absorbed in love; Krishna Himself stayed in his body for three months.” (CB, Antya 5.722–724)

This does not mean that the devotee became God. The Lord manifests Himself in the heart and body of His eternal servant, investing him with His power (avesha); the servant remains a servant, and that is why his words spoken “in the mood of the Lord” are not understood by everyone.

With Nityananda and Gadadhara Dasa, Abhirama came to Panihati, and first of all they visited the house of Raghava Pandita; the kirtana begun there filled the whole world with bliss. Murari Gupta relates that in Panihati Nityananda's friends — “Sri Rama, Sundara, Gauridasa” — appeared as cowherd boys, with flutes and horns; “Sri Rama” here is apparently he. According to Murari, from Badagachhi too, from Krishnadasa's house, Nityananda returned to Navadvipa “surrounded by Ramadasa and others” (“Krishna-chaitanya-charita” 4.23.22); this too is probably Abhirama.

There too, in Panihati, he was at the festival of flat rice and yogurt (chida-dadhi) that Raghunatha Dasa held for Nityananda. On the raised platform with Nityananda sat His companions:

“Ramadasa, Sundarananda, Gadadhara Dasa, Murari, Kamalakara, Sadashiva, Purandara.” (CC, Antya 6.61)

“Sri Ramadasa and the other cowherd boys were overwhelmed with love: on the bank of the Ganga they felt they were on the bank of the Yamuna.” (CC, Antya 6.90)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains in the “Anubhashya” that this Ramadasa is Abhirama Thakura, the cowherd boy.

The Power of Nityananda

At the command of Nityananda, who crushes godlessness, Abhirama Thakura became an acharya and preacher of bhakti; so writes Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya.” The biographies call him a mighty acharya and a great preacher of Gaudiya Vaishnavism: preaching bhakti at Nityananda's command, he delivered many godless men and opponents of the Vaishnava faith.

The old brahmana of Khanakula describes him to Srinivasa thus:

“The power of Abhirama Gosvami is formidable: seeing him, even invincible unbelievers tremble. He is ever mad with absorption in Nityananda; his charming mercy is known throughout the world.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 4.103–104)

The “Anubhashya” quotes these verses too. The biographies retell them so: the godless and the blasphemers feared him and fled at the mere sight of him, while he, invested with Nityananda's power, lived ever in rapture and showed mercy to all the fallen.

He is formidable only to godlessness. The power before which the godless tremble is Nityananda's power in him: Nityananda has invested His servant with His power (shakti-avesha) and acts through him, and the work of that power is not punishment but the deliverance of the fallen.

Malini

The “Bhakti-ratnakara” says that Abhirama was learned in all the shastras, supremely charming, and without equal in dance, song and instrumental music (4.106); the biographies call him a remarkable scholar.

His wife was Sri Malini-devi, the daughter of a brahmana. Abhirama married by the will of Nityananda-Balarama, taking a wife from the house of a learned brahmana. The narrator of the “Bhakti-ratnakara” says to Srinivasa:

“O Srinivasa, how much shall I tell you? He descended in a brahmana's house to deliver living beings. <…> By the will of Prabhu Nityananda-Balarama he married, [taking a wife] from the house of a learned brahmana. Sri Abhirama's wife is named Sri Malini; I cannot tell all her glory.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 4.105–108)

Malini is not a wife in the worldly sense but a partner in his service: together with her husband and their people she joyfully serves Sri Gopinatha (4.119), together with him she bestows mercy on Srinivasa and Narottama, and Vedagarbha in his verse honours Abhirama as “the husband of Sri Malini.” They lived at Khanakula-Krishnanagara.

Gopinatha and Rama-kunda

Abhirama longed to serve the Deity, and the Lord Himself came to him. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” relates:

“Gopinatha appeared to him as if in a dream, said, ‘Here I abide,’ and showed him the place. Digging at that place, Abhirama found the incomparable Deity of Gopinatha.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 4.114–115)

The news spread everywhere; people came running for darshan and, the moment they saw Gopinatha, forgot their grief. The pond where Gopinatha appeared came to be known far and wide as Rama-kunda: bathing in it and drinking its water, all were overwhelmed with bliss, and there was no counting the pilgrims (4.116–118). Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya” records the tradition that the Deity appeared when a pond was being dug in front of the temple, and that the pond has been called Abhirama-kunda ever since. One of the biographies tells that Gopinatha said to Abhirama in a dream that He wished to appear at Khanakula-Krishnanagara and lay hidden in the earth, and told him to dig Him out and begin His service; at the place Gopinatha showed, Abhirama found the Deity who captivates the mind.5

The service of Gopinatha was revealed in Gauda-mandala by Abhirama Thakura, in Kshetra-mandala, at Puri, by Gadadhara Pandita, and in Vraja by Madhu Pandita; the biographies name these three Gopinathas together.

Khanakula-Krishnanagara, Abhirama's shripata, stands on the bank of the river Khana, or Dvarakeshvara (kula means “bank”), in the Hooghly district; in the “Bhakti-ratnakara” the river is called Darukeshvara, and the country around Khanakula Virloka. According to one of the biographies, the place is called Krishnanagara because it has a temple of Krishna. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya” also describes the way there as it was in his time: by the Howrah–Amta railway to Champadanga station, and from there about ten miles south-west, past the market of Helanar Hat; in the rains the road floods, and then one goes by steamer from Kolaghat to Ranichak, and from there seven and a half miles north.

At the temple gate grows a bakula tree, and the spot is called Siddha-bakula-kunja; the story goes that on coming to the village Abhirama Thakura first sat down just here; according to another biography, he loved to sit under this tree.

As the “Anubhashya” describes it, the temple is the abode of Sri Baladeva, Sri Madana-mohana — alone, without Radha — and Sri Gopinatha. Gopinatha is carved on a single slab of touchstone (kashtipathar) a cubit and a quarter high and about a cubit wide, and on the same slab are the pastime of stealing the gopis' garments, a kadamba tree, the Yamuna, cows and calves: such is the archa-vigraha here. On the throne there are also the shri-murti of Abhirama Thakura himself, poised in the rapture of dance, and Sri Vraja-vallabha — the Divine Couple; there are also a shalagrama-shila and Sri Gopala.

Directly south of the present temple stands the old nine-spired (navaratna) temple. On a stone at the top the year of building is carved — 1181 of the Bengali era (about 1774–1775) — but there is no builder's name; it is said that Nachhirama Simha of the cowherd community of a neighbouring village built it. Formerly the Deity resided in this temple, and before it was built, on the same spot, in a thatched hut.

The inscription on the present temple reads: “The temple of Sri Sri Gopinatha Jiu built in Magha 1219, repaired in Vaishakha 1308” (about 1813 and 1901); its builder is said to be Pundarikaksha Raya of Madhavapura near Arambagh (Hooghly). In front of the old temple is a spacious brick natya-mandira; fishermen (dhivaras) of Medinipur built it in 1263 and restored it themselves in 1320 (about 1856–1857 and 1913–1914).6 Directly north of the Gopinatha temple stands the ancient temple of Sri Radha-vallabha Jiu, founded by local kayasthas of the Chaudhuri family.

According to the servants, as the “Anubhashya” reports them, since the days of Abhirama Thakura the Deity has been offered parboiled rice (siddha-chaul) and even puffed rice (muri); when the Thakura is laid down to rest, the temple doors are not closed, and everything is done in full view of all; the early-morning mangala-arati was no longer performed in his time. The servants then numbered thirty-six or thirty-seven families.

The Whip Jayamangala

Abhirama had a whip called “Sri Jayamangala.” Tradition says that whoever Abhirama Thakura touched with it awoke to love for Krishna.7 The touch of this whip is not a punishment but a gift of prema.

It is said that the whip is still kept in the temple, in an iron chest locked with the keys of all the servants together. It is two cubits long and wound with gold thread (jari). At the festival it is brought out only if all the servants agree.

It is said that the touch of Jayamangala, like Abhirama's obeisance, could be borne only by one who sincerely loves Krishna.

Srinivasa at Khanakula

When young Srinivasa, not yet an Acharya, came to Khardaha, Jahnava and Vasudha told him: “Go quickly to the house of Abhirama Gopala” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 4.93). According to the “Prema-vilasa,” Jahnava sent Ishana with him and a letter: she asked Abhirama to touch the youth three times with his whip.

On the way to Virloka an old brahmana of Khanakula joined Srinivasa. Learning who he was, the brahmana embraced him in tears and spoke at length about Abhirama: “Sri Thakura Abhirama is an abode of virtues; he will show you great mercy” (4.102); “Sri Thakura Abhirama is the embodiment of prema; all worship him — who does not proclaim his fame?” (4.111). At the end he warned: “Only the fortunate understand this inscrutable conduct; you will see it yourself, son — be careful” (4.126), and showed him the house.

Having bowed down, Srinivasa stayed waiting at the gate. Abhirama, in separation from the Lord, spoke to no one; but when he learned who had come, he smiled quietly and resolved to test his guest. He gave him ten “kards” of cowrie shells for his food; Srinivasa bought what was needed, cooked on the bank of the Darukeshvara and offered the meal to Krishna. Just then the Thakura sent four people to him; Srinivasa joyfully fed them and only then honoured the maha-prasada himself. Those who had been sent came back satisfied. “All these tests were to teach others,” remarks the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (4.130–138).8

Then Abhirama called him.

“With his whip named Jayamangala he touched Srinivasa's body three times.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 4.139)

As he touched him, he laughed aloud and said something to him. And when in loving rapture he was about to touch him once more, Malini-devi came and, smiling, held his hand:

“Restrain yourself, Gosani: there is no limit to the mercy you have shown. Srinivasa is only a boy; he will not be able to stay steady; if he goes mad with love, how will he accomplish his task?” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 4.142–143)

Malini is not quarrelling with her husband. She only reminds him that a great service lies ahead of the youth, and the mercy must be measured to it. Then both laid their hands on Srinivasa's head; he fell at their feet, and they raised him and bathed him in their tears.9

Srinivasa was filled with love for Krishna. Abhirama grew very fond of him and blessed him generously; Srinivasa did not take initiation from him, but became as good as a disciple to him, and the “Anubhashya,” listing Abhirama's disciples, calls him “half a disciple.” Both Abhirama and Malini entrusted him to the feet of Radha-Gopinatha and told him to go to Vrindavana, and in all the people of Krishnanagara and Khanakula love grew at the sight of Srinivasa (4.146–148). According to one of the biographies, Srinivasa humbly asked for his blessing to return to Shrikhanda.

The mercy of a Vaishnava is not bounded by the form of initiation: Srinivasa was not Abhirama's disciple, yet received so much love from him that he is counted almost a disciple. And the touch of “the transcendental whip of a pure devotee,” as one of the biographies calls it, gave him love for Krishna: so the mercy of a pure devotee makes another a devotee.

The Obeisance

Another tradition is connected with Abhirama's name, one that, in Srila Bhaktisiddhanta's words, is current to this day. If Abhirama bowed down before a stone or an image — before anything other than a Vishnu-shila or a Deity of Vishnu — it split apart and crumbled to dust. It is said that non-devotees, too, could not bear his obeisance, and one of the biographies adds that by his obeisance he would tell whether a Vishnu-shila or shalagrama was genuine: only a pure Vaishnava could withstand it, while for others it could prove fatal.10 The point of the tradition is not a destructive force. The obeisance of Krishna's cowherd friend, full of sakhya-bhava, can be received only by the Lord Himself, by His Deity and by His eternal associates; a stone that could not bear it was never a Deity.

So, tradition holds, the Lord revealed to the world the divinity of Nityananda's children. Abhirama's obeisance was received by His son Virabhadra (Virachandra) Gosvami and His daughter Sri Gangamata Gosvamini (Ganga-devi), and this confirmed that They were no ordinary persons. This is told also in two compositions of Abhirama himself, the “Sri Virabhadrashtaka” and the “Ganga-stotra.” Later books, the “Prema-vilasa” and the “Nityananda-vamsha-vistara,” tell more: after Abhirama's obeisances seven sons of Nityananda did not remain in this world, while Vira and Ganga, portions of the Lord Himself, remained; Abhirama prostrated himself three times before the infant Virachandra, the child smiled, and Abhirama recognized in Him Gauranga. The “Vaishnava-vandana” says that the Lord's secret design concerning Virachandra “Abhirama understood and revealed.” These are late testimonies, and we pass them on as tradition.

Tradition also links Abhirama's obeisance with the young Gopala Guru. According to one of the biographies, Abhirama came to Puri to test the boy with his obeisance, and the Vaishnavas grew alarmed; but Mahaprabhu set His foot on Gopala's forehead — whence the tilaka of his line — and took him on His lap, and the obeisance did him no harm.

And Raghunandana of Shrikhanda it was Abhirama who revealed to the world. Lochana Dasa recalls him:

“He to whom Chaitanya said, ‘You are My life,’ whom Abhirama Gosvami revealed, making known that he was the avatara of Madana — and all saw him so on Chaitanya's lap.” (Lochana Dasa, “Chaitanya-mangala,” Sutra-khanda 651–652)

Madana here is not the worldly god of love: the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” (70) calls Raghunandana Pradyumna, an eternal associate of Krishna.

In a song of Uddhava Dasa, Abhirama comes to Shrikhanda in search of Raghunandana. The boy's father, Mukunda Dasa, afraid of his obeisance, hides his son; but Raghunandana meets Abhirama at Baradangi, withstands his mighty obeisance, and together they sing the names of Gaura and Nityananda and dance. From that dance, tradition says, an ankle bell flew from Raghunandana's foot and dropped into a pond at Akai-hata — Nupura-kunda.11 And the “Nityananda-vamsha-vistara” says that the Deity Madana-mohana is bent more than usual — “from Abhirama's obeisance.”

Both the obeisance and the whip of Abhirama reveal the truth. The obeisance shows who is truly Vishnu or His eternal portion, as Virachandra and Ganga are; the whip bestows prema, and in such fullness that even Srinivasa could not have borne more.

Separation

When Nityananda withdrew from sight, Abhirama changed. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” says that from then on he constantly sighed deeply and spoke to no one: “in separation from Sri Prabhu he is always absorbed in love” (4.125, 4.131). This is not dejection or worldly grief: so an eternal associate of the Lord lives through separation (vipralambha), and it is the highest state of love.

So Narottama Dasa found him when, on his way to Nilachala, he came to Khanakula-Krishnanagara and bowed at his feet. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” (8.223–227) relates: in separation from Nityananda, Abhirama was hardly aware of the outer world, and so too was the incomparable Sri Malini. Seeing his state, Narottama was bathed in tears. He saw the wondrous Deity of Gopinatha and, seeing His service, was overcome with feeling; one of the biographies adds that he recited prayers before Gopinatha. Abhirama together with Malini showed him much mercy and told him to go quickly to Nilachala, and in the morning Narottama took his leave. According to the same biography, Abhirama pined in separation from both Gaura and Nityananda, and in the same separation lived Gadadhara Dasa.12

Disciples and Legacy

Of Abhirama's disciples the first known by name is Vedagarbha Acharya, whose verse the “Bhakti-ratnakara” quotes. A full list is given by Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya” on CC, Adi 11.13, after the book “Shakha-nirnaya” compiled by one Abhiramadasa, a disciple of Ratneshvara.13 There are twenty-four disciples, each with his place: Krishnadasa Thakura — Khanakula (his line has died out); Vedagarbha — Kayara, about ten miles south-west of Bardhaman (his descendants serve the Deity); Haridasa — Burhan; Pakhiya-Gopaladasa — Helal near Khanakula (a ruined temple, a “samaja,” is there); Gumphanarayana — Paikamajita near Ramajivanapura in Medinipur (descendants living); Dariya Mohana — Sitanagara; Satyaraghava — Mayanamuri in Bankura; Rajani Pandita — Salikha; Sundarananda — Bhangamora near Tarakeshvara (he has descendants); Krishnananda Avadhuta — Dvipagrama; Rangana-Krishnadasa — Sonatala; Muraridasa — Maldah; Mohana Thakura — Panihati; Yadu Haldar — Radhanagara south of the shripata (his line has died out, and his Deity of Balarama is served together with Gopinatha); Harimadhava — Anantanagara; Gopaladasa — Mahesh; Achyuta Pandita — Kotara (a descendant living); Lakshminarayana — Patala; Gopinathadasa — Puri; Nandakishora — Chunakhali pargana; Vidura Brahmachari — Patagrama (descendants living); Ramakrishna — Vinupara; Kamalakara — Gaurangapura, about four miles to the north (a samaja is there, and his descendants serve Nitai-Gaura); Balarama Thakura — Vishvagrama. Twenty-fifth, as “half a disciple,” Srinivasa Acharya is named.

Abhirama's descendants — by birth or by the line of disciples, the source does not say — live at Krishnanagara and Amta, and also at Vishnupura, Kotalpura and other villages of the Bankura district.

Many say that Abhirama founded the Bali Math in Puri.

Besides the “Virabhadrashtaka” and the “Ganga-stotra,” the “Pata-paryatana” (“Shripata-paryatana”) is ascribed to him — a description of the holy places of Gauda which mentions, among other things, “Raghava's bags.”14 There was also a biography, the “Abhirama-lilamrita”; it is named among the sources on Shyamananda, but we do not have the text of this book.

Abhirama's blessing, in Jayananda's words, rests also on his “Chaitanya-mangala”: the poet spreads his song by the garland-prasada of Virabhadra and the blessing of Abhirama, at the command of Gadadhara Pandita.

Great Vaishnavas visited Abhirama's shripata. Besides Srinivasa and Narottama, Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura came here in his travels of 1877–1910. And when Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati was going round Gaura-mandala, the temple servants received him and his companions with great warmth and special honour. So Abhirama's shripata is linked with the Sarasvata line as well.

The Cowherd Boy in the Padas and Later Tradition

The padas see Abhirama beside the Lord already in Navadvipa. In Vamshivadana's song Nityananda blows through His lips as on a horn, and at the call Gauridasa and Abhirama come running; in Vamshidasa's, Abhirama-Shridama drives the cows, and with him is Gauridasa-Subala; in Vasu Ghosha's, Abhirama stands at the door and calls Gaura to the pasture. Another pada tells how Abhirama weeps when Nityananda dances in Shrivasa's courtyard; in Narahari's he gives his shoulder to Nityananda, who cannot stand for love; in Ramachandra Dasa's he sings with Kashishvara, Purushottama and Narahari while the Lord dances. A pada quoted in the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (12.2578) says: prema flows from the eyes of Thakura Abhirama, and again and again he cries, “Hari! Hari!” Neither the “Charitamrita” nor the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” says directly that Abhirama was with the Lord in Navadvipa; this is the testimony of the padas, and not all of them are early.

Later biographies add stories of their own. The “Nityananda-vamsha-vistara” relates, from the words of Uddharana Datta: once in Vrindavana Nityananda the avadhuta called, “My brother, Shridama!” — and a cowherd boy came out of Govardhana; he did not recognize the shaven-headed Balarama, and then Nityananda showed His white form with plough and club and told him to “grow up” — so he became Abhirama Gopala. This is a late image of the meeting of eternal friends, not a tale of transformation: Shridama is eternally the friend of Krishna and Balarama and only appeared in a new form for Gaura's pastimes. According to the “Nityananda-vamsha-vistara” and the “Prema-vilasa,” when young Virabhadra secretly set off by boat to Advaita for a mantra, Jahnava sent Abhirama to bring Him back; Abhirama threw his flute and smashed the boat, and Virabhadra received initiation from Jahnava. The same “Nityananda-vamsha-vistara” says that in Nilachala Abhirama introduced Sarvabhauma and the Lord's associates to Virachandra, though chronologically this is doubtful. Jayananda writes that after the Lord's sannyasa Nityananda left Navadvipa with Ramadasa, Parameshvara and Sundarananda, and that when news came of the Lord's disappearance, “Ramadasa and the companions were struck dumb.”

Narahari Chakravarti, in the “Namamrita-samudra,” his prayers to the Lord's associates, asks the formidable Abhirama for protection:

“O Abhirama! This I say to you: protect me from the godless asuras.” (“Namamrita-samudra” 64)

Departure

Abhirama Thakura left this world on the krishna-saptami of the month of Chaitra — the seventh lunar day of the dark fortnight of Madhusudana-masa; so say Srila Bhaktisiddhanta and the biographies, and the same day is marked in the calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math as the Disappearance Day of Srila Abhirama Thakura (in 2026, 9 April). The year, the circumstances of his departure and the place of his samadhi the sources do not name.

On that day a great festival is held at Khanakula-Krishnanagara, and thousands of devotees gather.

Significance

Abhirama Thakura is Shridama, Krishna's eternal friend, the first of Nityananda's twelve gopalas, who descended into Gaura's pastimes. Sri Chaitanya sent him with Nityananda to preach in Gauda, and so he belongs to both circles. Everything extraordinary in him — the log-flute, the formidable obeisance, the whip that bestows prema — comes from the fullness of sakhya-prema and from the power of Nityananda with which He invested His servant. Formidable to godlessness, he was generous to the fallen; Srinivasa, without being his disciple, received love for Krishna from him; and after Nityananda's disappearance he lived in a silent separation that is itself the highest love. The Deity of Gopinatha, who revealed Himself to him at Khanakula, accepts service to this day.
